parts.text: "Here is a research idea, the card a planner wrote for it, and a check of which existing research or industrial programmes would use its result, with the gaps that check found. Root question: What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one? Idea: {\"title\":\"Drift probes on the autoformalizer\",\"text\":\"Probe the autoformalizer's activations while it writes definitions and statements, to flag when it has quietly strengthened a hypothesis or guessed a convention. In math, generators often 'know' they are wrong: a linear probe predicts trace correctness at 0.953 AUROC on MATH-500, against 0.674 for verbalized confidence. But transfer to other domains is weak (0.54/0.55 from MATH to ARC), the signal is 'diagnostic, not causal', and the only interp study of autoformalization (SMT-LIB, not Lean) gets 0.960 against a solver oracle but 0.679 against an LLM proxy for intent. No one has measured this on Lean, and the labels it needs are the human audit itself.\",\"root_link\":\"B4 / framer 4.3: whether a misformalization of the root statement or its definitions, which the kernel cannot see, leaves a readable trace inside the generator, which would shrink the human audit set.\",\"compute_open\":\"Quantity is models and labelled statements analysed. The most reported is nine models up to 72B on 100 training and 200 held-out math problems (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09502v1) and 950 SMT-LIB encodings (https://arxiv.org/html/2609.11085v2). Unknown above that: whether Lean statement drift is linearly readable in any model at all, and how a probe scores against human rather than solver or LLM-proxy intent labels.\",\"sequential\":\"The chain is: expert-labelled faithful/unfaithful pairs, then one forward pass per statement to cache activations, then a probe fit (minutes on a fraction of one GPU), then held-out evaluation. That is about 4 steps, with one run per model and realistically per subfield. Only the labelling step is serial (it is the expert audit). Labels could arrive in parallel if faithful statements were perturbed synthetically in targeted directions, as BPF's counterfactual probe generation does (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16541). That pays off only if probes trained on synthetic drift transfer to natural misformalizations. The nearest precedent is Goodfire's Rakuten SAE probes, trained on synthetic data, which held up on real production data (https://www.goodfire.com/research/rakuten-sae-probes-for-pii-detection).\"} Card: **I1 · Drift probes on the autoformalizer.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: unsure · REJECT **Question.** Can a linear probe read Lean autoformalization drift from generator activations, and does synthetic-drift training transfer to human-audited natural misformalizations? **What is known.** A linear SAE probe reached 0.960 AUROC against an SMT-LIB solver oracle but 0.679 against intent labels; largest compute: 950 encodings, one 27B verifier. No one has measured drift readability in Lean (only SMT-LIB), scored a probe against human audit labels, or tested synthetic-to-natural drift transfer. **Hypothesis.** Generators encode drift they cannot verbalize: a linear probe predicts trace correctness at 0.953, so Lean misformalizations should be linearly readable. **Restructuring.** Expert-labelled faithful/drifted pairs, one forward pass per statement, probe fit, held-out evaluation — four steps. Synthetic drift is generated in parallel by counterfactual perturbation, and forward passes over many statements run side-by-side on separate GPUs. **If compute is the lever.** Synthetic-drift probes transfer to natural Lean misformalizations: parallel GPUs reach AUROC ≥ 0.80 at 5,000 statement-runs, sooner than one sequential GPU. **If not.** Drift is weakly readable in Lean: probe AUROC on natural misformalizations stays near 0.679 even at 150,000 statement-runs, so it never crosses the flagging threshold. **Test.** Cache a 7B Lean autoformalizer's hidden states over 100k+ runs; train logistic probes on synthetic drift, test on 200 human-audited natural misformalizations; time parallel 4-GPU vs sequential and sharded-copy baselines; compare AUROC to SMT-LIB 0.960/0.679. *Compute axis.* Statement-runs (forward passes whose activations are cached and probed): 2,000–150,000 statement-runs, 3 levels. Closest prior: 950 [s_genv_oracle], beyond it. **Check first.** Planted synthetic-drift probe hits AUROC ≥ 0.90; 4-shard parallel caching matches single-GPU sequential caching within ±0.05 AUROC; shuffle control 0.50. **Would not show.** Shows readability, not a causal fix, and only within Lean. Cannot prove synthetic-to-natural transfer beyond the audited 200 pairs. *Cost.* Plans $489.21 of the $1,000 budget over 198 machine-hours, leaving $510.79. Main guess: 7B generation throughput [g], measured after $2.18 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 3.2× lower. Kimina's ~1,000-problem human-curated set (used to tune its judge prompt) is the closest artefact but is private, so the card's held-out real-error set must be built independently.\",\"DeepMind's formalizer is a closed Gemini model: the card's probe methodology requires activation access, so results on open 7B/8B/32B formalizers transfer to AlphaProof only if run internally.\",\"FormalAlign is the only hidden-state-based alignment work found, and it is a separately fine-tuned 7B evaluator trained on a contrastive loss over synthetic misalignments — not frozen-model linear probes; the card's cross-model probe-transfer arm ('copied across models') is untested by any programme.\",\"The card is scoped to competition and conjecture statements; the research-level definition formalization in the 2026 AlphaProof-Nexus programme (OEIS/Erdős problems) is at or beyond the card's stated test distribution, so the lever outcome there is extrapolation, not evidence.\",\"Goedel-Prover and Kimina both use external LLM judges (Qwen2.5-72B, QwQ-32B) plus ad-hoc safeguards (negation-proving, triviality filters); the card's comparison is against expert-label probes and text-only baselines, not against these production judge ensembles, so adoption decisions would need a head-to-head with the judges they actually run.\"] Propose three close variants of the idea.
